Expand University of Cape Town vice-chancellor Professor Mosa Moshabela is challenging four resolutions adopted by the UCT Council, as his lawyers press the university for answers over claims that some complaints investigated against him were fabricated. (Supplied) Story audio is generated using AI A former University of Cape Town staff member has called for an independent investigation after discovering that her name had allegedly been recorded as the source of a misconduct complaint against vice-chancellor Prof Mosa Moshabela — a complaint she says she never made. Moshabela has asked the Western Cape High Court to order the UCT council to cancel four resolutions he says were imposed on him unfairly following an investigation into 34 alleged complaints from staff and students about his behaviour. But Wilna Venter, who spent 18 years at the university, said she was shocked when Fairbridges Attorneys approached her in March and she learnt that she had been listed as the source of one of the complaints against Moshabela. In a statement, Venter said she had never lodged a complaint against Moshabela with UCT’s ombud’s office, the university, or anyone else, either directly or indirectly. Venter said she had never authorised anyone to lodge a complaint on her behalf and had never been unhappy with Moshabela’s conduct towards her or anyone else. “Any record that says otherwise is false, and I ask that it be corrected and withdrawn,” she said. Her account potentially adds weight to concerns raised separately by seven UCT council members, who alleged in an August 8 letter that some complaints investigated against Moshabela had been fabricated, that some purported complainants did not exist and that people recorded as complainants had denied lodging complaints. These allegations have not been independently established, and the investigators’ report has not been made public. Venter called for an independent investigation into how complaints against Moshabela were “solicited, gathered, recorded and attributed, by whom, and on whose instructions”, saying she would make herself available to such an inquiry. She also spoke strongly in support of Moshabela, describing him, based on her dealings with him, as a leader of “exceptional ability, of integrity, and of conviction”. Meanwhile, lawyers acting for Moshabela have stepped up pressure on the university to answer claims that some complaints against him were fabricated and that people recorded as complainants either did not exist or denied ever lodging complaints. In a series of letters to UCT’s lawyers, seen by the Sunday Times, lawyers representing Moshabela in his personal capacity demanded to know whether the university disputes an account by seven members of its council about the findings of the investigation into Moshabela. The lawyers have also demanded access to the investigators’ report and the preservation of documents potentially relevant to further litigation, while indicating that Moshabela could pursue civil action if allegations were falsely attributed to people who never made them. The legal salvo follows a letter written earlier this month by council members Ezra Davids, Brian Kantor, Tom Moultrie, Jacques Rousseau, Marlon Parker, Kessler Perumalsamy and Kelly Phelps. The letter is addressed to council chair Norman Arendse, the interim registrar and fellow council members. In it, the seven members alleged that an independent investigation had found that 34 complaints against Moshabela — including, they said, serious allegations such as sexual harassment — were without merit. “The independent investigation revealed that certain of the complaints put forward by the ombud were fabricated,” they wrote. They further claimed that investigators had indicated that their findings concerning the ombud were serious enough for disciplinary action to be considered. Moshabela’s lawyers said he had not seen the investigators’ report and therefore could not allege that any complaint had been fabricated, that a complainant did not exist or that anyone had acted improperly. Instead, his lawyers said they were recording the claims made by the seven council members and that if those accounts proved correct, Moshabela could pursue civil remedies against those responsible because he would have suffered ”grave injury to his dignity, his good name and his professional standing”. The letter was prompted by the postponement of a special council meeting scheduled for August 8 to continue discussions on the investigators’ report concerning Moshabela and the ombud. The seven council members criticised what they described as a delay of more than a month in completing discussions about the ombud and warned that the handling of the matter had placed UCT at legal and reputational risk. They also raised broader concerns about the relationship between Moshabela and the council, alleging that since at least March 2025, the council had obstructed the vice-chancellor in carrying out his executive functions and delayed the launch of his strategic plan. The council members further alleged that correspondence sent by Moshabela’s legal representatives to council had not reached them. “We were kept in the dark,” they wrote. They said they had seen correspondence between Moshabela’s lawyers and the council for the first time when it was included in his high court application. The seven called for the council to urgently address what they described as “critical lapses in governance” so members could fulfil their fiduciary duties and protect the university’s reputation. The council has in the meantime suspended implementation of the four resolutions challenged by Moshabela pending the outcome of his high court review. Among them was that the vice-chancellor undergo annual performance reviews. Arendse said the council would await Moshabela’s supplementary papers before deciding whether to oppose the application. The council has also indicated its willingness to participate in mediation. Arendse defended the process followed after concerns about Moshabela were brought to his attention, saying the ombud had alerted him to their existence and seriousness without compromising confidentiality. “I sought independent legal advice and thereafter placed the matter before council and informed the vice-chancellor,” he said. “The process that followed was undertaken on independent legal advice and was designed to ensure independence, appropriate confidentiality and fairness to all persons affected.” UCT said the ombud operated independently from the council and that confidentiality was fundamental to the office. Photograph: Andrew Leyden/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen Trump claimed his ban was due to the news organizations constantly reporting ‘fake news’. Photograph: Andrew Leyden/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock Donald Trump MS Now and CNN say their reporters were denied access to White House after Trump media ban President said he was banning MS Now, CNN and Politico journalists, saying of their coverage: ‘You get sick of it.’ Edward Helmore Sat 19 Sep 2026 10.39 EDT First published on Sat 19 Sep 2026 09.56 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google News outlets MS Now and CNN said their journalists were denied access to the White House grounds on Saturday morning, a day after Donald Trump said he would ban them ,and the website Politico from the executive branch complex. MS Now said a reporter and a cameraman had been denied access and had their White House press passes confiscated by the US Secret Service at a security gate outside the West Wing. CNN reported that its reporter Betsy Klein was also denied access and had her press pass seized too. “The White House belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded by our tax dollars,” MS Now said, adding that it “intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our first amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy. Trump’s battle to rename the Kennedy Center has put its future at risk Read more “We stand firmly behind our anchors, our reporters and our newsroom. We will continue to report on the president, the administration and the issues that impact the American people.” CNN said in a statement. “We have a right under the US constitution to do our reporting without hindrance or interference from the government and this ban is an illegal assault on this fundamental right.” Trump’s threat to banish CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House has brought condemnation from first amendment advocates and Democratic officials, among others, as the conflict between the US president and parts of the media sharply escalates ahead of November’s midterm elections. It has also thrown into stark relief Trump’s attack on press freedom in the US, which has unnerved civil liberties advocates. In a Truth Social post on Friday afternoon, Trump said he would order the removal of the news outlets “effective immediately” for what he claimed was “constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” and said he is considering banning more. Trump did not identify a single infraction, but rather said his decision was “really just cumulative stories over the last two years. You get sick of it.” The White House Correspondents’ Association, which represents the White House press corps, condemned the move. “The constitution protects the freedom of the press from government interference,” it said on social media. “That protection does not depend on whether the president likes a news organization’s coverage, agrees with its reporting or approves of the questions its journalists ask.” The body said the issue is “about more than the rights of journalists” but about “the right of the American people to receive a full and independent account of the activities, policies and decisions of whoever occupies the nation’s highest office”. Trump has long clashed with the media over what he considers slanted coverage of his administration and himself personally, as well as describing a media environment in which the press and his political opponents are in collusion. Last year the Associated Press was banned form the White House after refusing to acknowledge an executive order changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico to Gulf of America. After Friday’s ban was announced, CNN issued a statement saying that removing its reporters from the grounds could violate the law. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Around 2-3 times a day Sign up to Breaking News US Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “CNN stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting,” a spokesperson for the outlet said. “We have a right under the US constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government.” Politico also issued a statement, saying it would “continue to fairly report on this White House and future ones” and “will vigorously defend our first amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them”. Jim Acosta, a former CNN reporter, accused Trump of “taking a meat axe to the free press in this country”. Speaking on MS Now on Friday, Acosta called the latest media bans “a slippery slope” and warned: “We are on the path to having a state media-like system in this country.” Acosta said the media should collectively oppose Trump’s ban. “Each of these news organizations should sue the White House, sue Donald Trump , and that other news organizations in Washington should band together and say, ‘We will not go to the White House and cover you and cover your administration. We’re banning you .’” Press freedom group PEN America said: “Someone needs to explain to President Trump how the first amendment works. As we’ve seen time and time again, this administration’s hostility toward the press is never about the accuracy of news stories, but about its inability to withstand scrutiny of its actions. The White House can’t be allowed to decide which journalists are able to cover the president based on the content of their news coverage.” Explore more on these topics Donald Trump MS Now CNN Press freedom US constitution and civil liberties TV news Trump administration news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://jewishpress.com/ichthyological/.text: Categories: Torah / Names and Numen / Headline Mailbag #3 By Rabbi Reuven Chaim Klein | October 27, 2026, 9 AM ET (123rf.com) Print Share Ichthyological Possibility for Pesha QUESTION: Hi! In a not-so-recent column (“Name Mailbag,” Nov. 2025) you stated that the name Pesha is probably a Yiddish derivative of a Hebrew name such as Batya . My wife's middle name is Pesha and she had been under the impression that Pesha was the feminine of Fishel , meaning "fish.” Is there ANY possibility of this? Thanks. -Dr. M. Jacobson ANSWER: Your question put a smile on my face because my wife's grandmother is named Pesha Fischer (may she live until 120). From what I understand, the name Fishel (meaning "little fish") first developed as a kinnui for the Hebrew name Ephraim because the Biblical Ephraim was blessed by his grandfather Jacob that he should multiply like fish (Gen. 48:16). To say what you are proposing, the derivation scheme would be something like Fishel → Fish → Pish → Pesh → Pesha, which isn't so likely. From an onomastic and etymological perspective, this trajectory is problematic for several reasons. First, diminutives and feminines in Yiddish naming practice generally preserve a recognizable core of the original name. We often see suffixes added (-ke, -le, -el, -a), but wholesale replacement of initial consonants like a shift from f to p is highly unusual. Second, while Fishel does generate related forms (such as surnames Fish , Fischman , or Fisher ), there is no known pattern whereby an animal-based male kinnui names produces an independent female given name through semantic translation alone. In other words, Ashkenazic women were not typically named by creating a feminine counterpart to a symbolic male nickname (“fish” → “female fish-name”), especially when the result bears no obvious phonological resemblance to the original. By contrast, the phonetic evolution from Batya → Basya → Pesha is far more plausible within Eastern European Jewish speech patterns, where consonant softening and dialectal shifts are amply documented. I can't get more detailed because I'm already boring myself, but you can read about those types of onomastic morphologies in Alexander Beider's book A Dictionary of Ashkenazic Given Names: Their Origins, Structure, Pronunciation, and Migrations . So I can't say there is NO possibility of Pesha deriving from Fishel, but it doesn't seem likely given what we know of historical Jewish naming conventions. -RCK Chofetz Chaim’s Surname QUESTION: What was the Chofetz Chaim's last name — Cohen , Kagan , or Poupko ? -Shlomo Greenwald (Fair Lawn, NJ) ANSWER: Good question. I can see why it’s so confusing. In all his seforim , the Chofetz Chaim signed his name Yisroel Meir HaKohen, which might suggest that his surname was Cohen. But the truth is that in the area of Poland where he lived, the h-sound often morphed into a g-sound in names. For example, the town Horodna is also called Gorodna, the surname Horowitz becomes Gurwitz , the surname Heller becomes Geller , Helfand becomes Gelfand , Kohut becomes Kogut , Harry becomes Gary , and so forth. In the same way, for the Chofetz Chaim, the h-sound in the middle of Kohen becomes Kagan . Consequently, sources not written in Hebrew often refer to the Chofetz Chaim as Rabbi Yisroel Meir Kagan. But I’m not sure if it’s accurate to really say that Kagan was his surname. Additionally, while the Chofetz Chaim’s father might have been a Kohen/Kagan, his father died when he was young and his mother remarried. People say that her husband’s surname was Poupko and since the Chofetz Chaim grew up in the Poupko residence, he is also associated with that family name, which he may have adopted in certain contexts. But the truth is that his mother married Rabbi Shimon HaLevi Epstein. Instead, it seems that the Chofetz Chaim himself used the surname Poupko from childhood, and even his father and father's father used that surname. After corresponding with members of the greater Poupko family and descendants of the Chofetz Chaim, I wasn't able to get down to the bottom of the matter as to when/why he seemingly later switched out Poupko for Kagan. So basically, in some ways, all three options that you mentioned are correct. What makes things more complicated is that in the next generation, the Chofetz Chaim's two sons took on two different surnames: His oldest son Rabbi Aryeh Leib took on the Poupko last name, while his younger son Rabbi Aharon went by Kohen/Kagan . -RCK Avir/Abir QUESTION: Shalom, Reuven. We are searching for a boy's name to give, be’ezras Hashem , in few weeks and you are the only one I know who probably knows the answer to my question. Is it appropriate nowadays to give the name Abir, more precisely Abir Yaakov? I don't mean Adir nor Avir, but specifically Abir (based on the Biblical Hebrew word for "mighty/strong one"). Can you please have a look at the attached dictionary entry and give your opinion? Thank you in advance! By the way, we are planning on moving to Israel in a few years to join the Belz community in Jerusalem. -Eva Elias ANSWER: First let me reveal my bias in that I have a conservative view of naming conventions. I especially feel strongly that you should not give a name that your kid will be embarrassed about, for example, if they're the only kid in their class or in their school with that name. I also think that especially because you are a giyoret and you are an outsider trying to join a new Chassidic community, you don’t want to stick out even more by giving your son a weird name. So, I strongly advise against giving the name Abir . According to data from the Israeli Central Bureau of Statistics (CBS), the name Abir is quite rare in Israel. It only start being giving in the 1980s. And its all-time peak popularity was in 2021, when 35 boys born in Israel that year were given this name. In that year, it was ranked the #375 th most popular name given to Jewish boys in the Holy Land; not very popular. Also, the way the name Abir is written in unvowelized Hebrew, it is likely to end up being pronounced Avir (like the word is pronounced six times in Tanach, even though elsewhere it is read as Abir). That would make this name a homonym with the Hebrew word for “air.” You don't want your kid's name to sound like "air." Think of all the schoolyard bullying that the name is just asking for. Adir is a bit more conventional in Israeli circles, but I’ve never met anybody named Abir or Avir. Although, there is an Arabic feminine name Abir (also spelled Abeer ), which literally means "perfume/fragrant/aroma/beautiful smell." Again, I advise sticking to traditional names; what’s wrong with just Yaakov? The Baba Sali's grandfather Rabbi Yaakov Abuchatzeira (1806-1880) wrote a book called Abir Yaakov (although technically, it should probably be called Avir Yaakov based on how the phrase is vocalized in Tanach). -RCK POSTSCRIPT: A month after I sent this answer, I heard back from Mrs. Elias and she informed me that she had a healthy baby boy, and they gave him the name Shraga Yaakov at his bris . Jeremy QUESTION: Is Jeremy a Jewish name? -Jeremy G. ANSWER: Depends what you mean by a "Jewish name." Is it a name that some Jewish people have? Definitely. It's actually quite popular in American Jewish circles. There's even a famous American rosh yeshiva who recently made aliyah who goes by Jeremy (I wonder if he still does or has since Hebraicized his name). Is it a kodesh name that has a Hebrew origin? Well, sort of: It seems that Jeremy is an alternate form of the name Jeremiah , which as you probably know is an Anglicization of the Hebrew name Yirmiyahu found in Tanach. Jeremy is also the English name that my parents gave to my little brother Yerucham Klein, the world-famous Instagram food and travel influencer. -RCK The Prime Ministers QUESTION: I just found out that the last name of David Ben-Gurion (the first prime minister of Israel) was originally Green, not Ben-Gurion. What were the original last names of the other prime ministers? -Benny Blue. ANSWER: Yes! David Ben-Gurion is a particularly good example of the phenomenon. He was born David Grün (or Green), a perfectly ordinary German/Yiddish surname meaning “green.” He eventually adopted the Hebrew surname Ben-Gurion . This wasn't a Hebrew translation of Grün , however, rather it reflected an ideological Zionism, with the man who would become the first prime minister of Israel getting inspiration from the historical Jewish leader Yosef ben Gurion (one of the Jewish leaders associated with the revolt against Rome in the end of the Second Temple period, and also the penname of the author of Yossiphon ). The ideological Hebraization of names produced names that were sometimes phonetic adaptations, sometimes semantic translations, and sometimes completely new Hebrew names with an ancient-Israelite or biblical flavor. I even found a sefer on Otzar HaChochmah devoted to giving people guidelines for how to Hebraicize their old European names when they come to Israel. Among Israel's prime ministers, there are quite a few examples of this onomastic phenomenon. Moshe Sharett was born Moshe Chertok (Shertok); Levi Eshkol was Levi Shkolnik ; Golda Meir was Golda Mabovitch ; Yitzhak Shamir was born Yitzhak Yezernitsky (Jaziernicki); Shimon Peres was Szymon Perski ; Ehud Barak was Ehud Brog ; Ariel Sharon was Ariel Scheinerman ; and Yair Lapid inherited the Hebrew surname Lapid after his father changed the family's earlier name Lampel . Some of these name-changes are themselves rather interesting. Shkolnik (Skolnik) is connected with the Slavic word for “school,” but bears a phonetic similarity to the Hebrew word e shkol ("grape cluster"). Similarly, Brog sounds a bit like Barak, so that connection is also phonetic. Peres's original last name Perski is a Polish-form surname, and Slavic names ending in -ski/-sky very often indicated an association with a place or locality. But it became Peres, after the Hebrew word peres in Chumash for a non-kosher bird of prey (possibly a "vulture"). Scheinerman is German/Yiddish in form, with schein meaning something like “beautiful,” “bright,” or “fair-looking.” If you take some of the consonants from Scheinerman and re-arrange them, you get Shamir (the name of the mythical worm that King Solomon used to cut the stones for the Temple). A particularly neat example is Lapid: The Jewish surname Lampel is etymologically related to the English word lamp. I even have the name in my family tree, as one of my great-great-grandfathers was named Ezriel Lampl. The name Lapid comes from the Biblical Hebrew word lapid , which means “torch,” so the example of former prime minister Yair Lapid's surname actually preserves the basic meaning and imagery of the old name, while giving it a Hebrew form. And Benjamin Netanyahu's story is interesting in a different way: his father was born Benzion Mileikowsky (1910-2012), but he adopted the name Netanyahu as a nod to his own father, Rabbi Nathan Mileikowsky (1879-1935). -RCK The Name Disha QUESTION: Hi. I very much enjoyed your articles in The Jewish Press on names. I was wondering if you know the origin of the name Disha, which was my mother's name. She was from Poland. Across the years, we have come across a few people with that name. Thank you and Gmar chasima tova . -Leah Preiserowicz (Brooklyn, NY) ANSWER: I actually dealt with this name in an earlier column that asked about the name Tisha. Basically, it's related to word for "soul" in various Slavic languages. See "Name Mailbag" (Nov. 2025).
